name: Chandrayaan-3
description: India's 2023 Moon mission (plus 4 distractor passages on other ISRO missions).

passages.title: Chandrayaan-3 mission overview
passages.text: Chandrayaan-3 is the third lunar exploration mission of the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO). It was designed as a follow-on to Chandrayaan-2 to demonstrate safe landing and roving on the lunar surface. The mission consists of a lander module named Vikram, a rover named Pragyan and a propulsion module.

passages.title: Launch of Chandrayaan-3 from Sriharikota
passages.text: Chandrayaan-3 was launched on 14 July 2023 at 2:35 pm IST from the Second Launch Pad of the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh. The spacecraft was carried into orbit by the LVM3-M4 rocket.

passages.title: LVM3 launch vehicle
passages.text: The LVM3 (Launch Vehicle Mark-3), formerly known as GSLV Mk III, is a three-stage heavy-lift launch vehicle developed by ISRO. Its flight designated LVM3-M4 placed the Chandrayaan-3 spacecraft into an elliptical parking orbit around Earth.

passages.title: Lunar orbit insertion and lander separation
passages.text: After a series of orbit-raising manoeuvres and a trans-lunar injection, Chandrayaan-3 entered lunar orbit on 5 August 2023. Its orbit around the Moon was then reduced in steps. The lander module separated from the propulsion module on 17 August 2023.

passages.title: Vikram lander touches down near the lunar south pole
passages.text: The Vikram lander of Chandrayaan-3 soft-landed on the Moon on 23 August 2023, shortly after 6 pm IST. The landing site is in the high-latitude region near the lunar south pole, at roughly 69 degrees south latitude.

passages.title: India's place in lunar landing history
passages.text: With the Chandrayaan-3 landing, India became the fourth country to achieve a soft landing on the Moon, after the Soviet Union, the United States and China. India also became the first country to land a spacecraft near the lunar south pole.

passages.title: Vikram lander and its payloads
passages.text: The Chandrayaan-3 lander is named Vikram, after Vikram Sarabhai, who is widely regarded as the founder of the Indian space programme. The lander carried scientific instruments including RAMBHA-LP, ChaSTE and ILSA, along with a passive Laser Retroreflector Array provided by NASA.

passages.title: Pragyan rover
passages.text: Pragyan is the rover of the Chandrayaan-3 mission. It is a six-wheeled rover weighing about 26 kg that rolled down a ramp from the Vikram lander after touchdown. It carried two instruments, the Alpha Particle X-ray Spectrometer (APXS) and the Laser Induced Breakdown Spectroscope (LIBS).

passages.title: Designed mission life of the lander and rover
passages.text: The Vikram lander and Pragyan rover were designed to operate for one lunar day, which is about 14 Earth days. Both are solar powered and were not designed to survive the extremely cold lunar night.

passages.title: Sulphur detected on the lunar surface by Pragyan
passages.text: Instruments on the Pragyan rover carried out in-situ studies near the lunar south pole and confirmed the presence of sulphur on the lunar surface through direct elemental analysis. The rover's LIBS instrument also detected elements such as aluminium, calcium, iron, chromium, titanium, manganese, silicon and oxygen.

passages.title: ChaSTE temperature measurements
passages.text: The ChaSTE instrument on the Vikram lander measured the temperature profile of the lunar topsoil near the south pole, probing to a depth of about 10 cm. ISRO released the first graph of these temperature variations on 27 August 2023.

passages.title: Rover traverse and sleep mode
passages.text: The Pragyan rover traversed over 100 metres on the lunar surface before it was put into sleep mode on 2 September 2023. The Vikram lander was put into sleep mode on 4 September 2023. ISRO later tried to re-establish contact after the lunar night, but neither the lander nor the rover woke up.

passages.title: Vikram hop experiment
passages.text: On 3 September 2023, the Vikram lander performed a hop experiment. On command, it fired its engines, rose about 40 cm and landed safely about 30 to 40 cm away from its original position.

passages.title: Shiv Shakti point and National Space Day
passages.text: The Chandrayaan-3 landing site on the Moon was named the Shiv Shakti point. The Government of India declared 23 August, the date of the landing, as National Space Day, and the first National Space Day was celebrated on 23 August 2024.

passages.title: Propulsion module and its return to Earth orbit
passages.text: The Chandrayaan-3 propulsion module carried the SHAPE payload, designed to study Earth from lunar orbit. In late 2023, ISRO moved the propulsion module out of lunar orbit and back into an orbit around Earth, using fuel left over from the mission.

passages.title: Chandrayaan-2 background
passages.text: Chandrayaan-2 was launched on 22 July 2019. Its lander crash-landed on the Moon during its descent in September 2019, but its orbiter continued to operate. The Chandrayaan-2 orbiter later served as a communication backup for the Chandrayaan-3 lander.

passages.title: Aditya-L1 launch
passages.text: Aditya-L1 is India's first space-based solar observatory. It was launched on 2 September 2023 aboard the PSLV-C57 rocket from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota.

passages.title: Aditya-L1 halo orbit insertion
passages.text: On 6 January 2024, Aditya-L1 was inserted into a halo orbit around the first Sun-Earth Lagrange point (L1), about 1.5 million km from Earth. From this position the spacecraft can observe the Sun continuously without being blocked by eclipses.

passages.title: Aditya-L1 scientific payloads
passages.text: Aditya-L1 carries seven scientific payloads to study the Sun. They include the Visible Emission Line Coronagraph (VELC) and the Solar Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope (SUIT), which observe the solar corona and photosphere, as well as instruments that measure the solar wind.

passages.title: Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan)
passages.text: The Mars Orbiter Mission, also called Mangalyaan, was launched by ISRO on 5 November 2013 aboard a PSLV rocket. It entered orbit around Mars on 24 September 2014, making India the first Asian nation to reach Mars orbit and the first nation to do so on its maiden attempt.
